1.12.m:
When [he contemplated] the bliss-bestowing Brahman, the Lord who destroys affliction,
which is inside Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the sun, and beyond the senses,

having attained peace through his own mind, Atri remained in self-restraint;
[such was] the majesty of his austerity, which bestows supreme bliss.

Because the lord of the dynasty presided over it together with the established agreement,
and having seen him, he beheld him with Soma, therefore the all-pervading Soma came to be.
Then from [Atri's] two eyes flowed water born of Atri, / illuminating the entire universe, with its mobile and immobile beings, with moonlight.
Then the quarters of the sky, possessing desire, received it in the form of women; / having become an embryo, that [seed] born of Atri remained in their wombs.
Then the quarters of the sky, unable to bear it, discharged the embryo; / thereupon the four-faced [Brahmā], taking up that embryo and uniting it into one,
Brahmā made him into a young man, bearing all weapons. / Then, on a chariot equipped with a thousand horses and consisting of the power of the Veda, the Lord,
placing him [on it], that Grandfather took him to his own world. / Then it was proclaimed by the Brahman-seers: "Indeed, let him become our master."
As he was being praised by seers, gods, gandharvas, and likewise apsarases, / his great pre-eminence increased further.
From the canopy of his splendour, the host of divine herbs arose on earth; / therefore his radiance is always greater at night.
For that reason Soma became the lord of herbs, and he is indeed counted among the twice-born. / His essence is the abode of the Vedas, which is this auspicious orb.
It wanes and waxes always in the dark and bright fortnights. / Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave seven and twenty
maidens to him, endowed with beauty and charm, exceedingly radiant. / Then, for ten thousands of thousands of years,
the cool-rayed [moon] performed austerities, intent solely on meditation upon Viṣṇu. / Then the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, was pleased with him,
and Janārdana, the supreme self, said: "Choose a boon." / Then Soma chose the boon: "May I sacrifice in the world of Śakra.
May the four classes of hosts of gods, beginning with Brahmā, / be visibly the recipients of the offering in my abode at the Rājasūya;
and may Hara, the trident-bearer, be our guardian god." / Told "So be it" by Viṣṇu, he then undertook the Rājasūya.
Atri was the hotṛ, Bhṛgu the adhvaryu, and the four-faced [Brahmā] the udgātṛ; / Hari himself became his brahman-priest and overseer.
All the gods were the members of the assembly, according to the prescribed rule for the Rājasūya; / likewise the Vasus were the adhvaryu-priests, and so were the Viśvedevas.
The three worlds were given by him as the sacrificial fee to the officiating priests. / Then, having attained sovereignty that is hard to attain and honoured by creation,
having at that time attained the sole lordship over the seven worlds through his own austerity, / once, as he was walking in a pleasure garden, he saw [a woman] adorned with many flower-ornaments,

fatigued by the weight of her broad hips and breasts, her limbs excessively delicate even in plucking flowers, / the wife of the preceptor of the gods, with long, beautiful eyes that delighted the arrows of the bodiless Love;
that lord of the stars, afflicted by love, seized Tārā by the hair in a secluded place; / she too, afflicted by love, took delight with him, her mind completely captivated by the charm of his form.
Then, having disported for a long time, the moon took Tārā and went to his own home; / yet even in his own home there was no satisfaction for him who was devoted to Tārā when pleasures arrived.

Bṛhaspati, burned by the fire of separation from her, became single-minded in steadfast meditation on her; / but he was unable to utter a curse against him, nor, with mantras, weapons, fire, and many poisons,
was the lord of speech able to harm him by various means or magical practices. / Then, tormented by love, he begged the god Soma for his wife.

Though being begged by Maheśvara, by the four-faced [Brahmā], by the Sādhyas, / the Maruts, together with the world-protectors, he did not surrender the wife of Bṛhaspati, infatuated under the sway of desire.
When the moon would in no way surrender her, Śiva became filled with wrath— / he who is renowned on earth as Vāmadeva, whose lotus feet are worshipped by many Rudras.

Then Giriśa, bearer of the Pināka, his disciple, bound by the bond of affection for Bṛhaspati, / taking up his bow Ājagava, the foe of Tripura set out, attended by the lords of beings and the perfected beings,
to fight with Soma, exceptionally radiant, his face terrifying with the fire of his third eye. / And eighty terrible-formed troop-leaders of the hosts of Gaṇas marched along with him;
accompanied by many hosts of the lords of yakṣas situated in chariots, / with a padma of vetālas, yakṣas, uragas, and kinnaras, and likewise with one hundred million

and three hundred and twelve [other] chariots. Soma too went there, his anger greatly increased, / his splendour heightened by Śanaiścara and Aṅgāraka, accompanied by an army of constellations, daityas, and asuras.
The seven worlds, containing the earth, forests, islands, and oceans, were terrified. / The bearer of the Pināka advanced right toward Soma, seizing a vast fire of blazing weapons.
Then arose that great battle between the two armies, fearful, terrible, and moonlike, / which caused the destruction of all beings, intensified, sharp and fierce, of the single form of blazing fire.
Then the entire army of both sides went to destruction by one another's fierce and sharp weapons; / blazing weapons fell in that manner, thoroughly burning heaven, earth, and the underworld.
Rudra released the head-of-Brahma weapon out of anger, and Soma too [released] the Soma weapon of unfailing power; / by the impact of the two, fear arose in the ocean, the earth, and the sky.
Then the Grandfather, seeing the fierce battle progressing toward the destruction of the worlds, / intervened with great effort along with the gods and restrained [them]:

"Why are you causing the destruction of people without a cause, O Soma? An improper act has been committed by you, / since an exceedingly terrifying war has been waged by you to abduct another's wife, O Soma!
You will become an inauspicious planet among people, and you are exceedingly sinful toward those who eat through the mouth of fire; / return this wife to the lord of speech, honouring my word!"
Saying "So be it," the garlanded with cool rays withdrew from the battle, and from that moment became calmed. / Then Bṛhaspati, taking Tārā, went happily to his own home, and Rudra did as well.
Pulastya said: / Then, at the end of a year, resembling twelve suns, / wearing divine yellow garments, adorned with divine ornaments,
a youth emerged from Tārā's womb, resembling the sun, / knowing all the treatises on statecraft, learned, the originator of the treatise on elephants.
By name this prince was renowned as a royal physician; / because he was the son of king Soma, Budha is traditionally called the prince.
The mighty one eclipsed all the splendours of the people. / Brahmā and the other gods arrived there along with divine seers,
all of them at the house of Bṛhaspati on the occasion of the birth ceremony. / Then the gods asked Tārā: "By whom was the boy begotten?"
Then, being ashamed, she said nothing at all to them at that time. / When questioned again and again, the excellent woman, bashfully,
said after a long time: "By Soma." Then the moon took the son, / gave him the name Budha, and bestowed a kingdom upon the earth.
Then, having performed the consecration, the all-pervading lord made a grant: / having assigned him the middle of the planets, Brahmā, along with the Brahman-seers,
vanished right there while all living beings were watching. / And upon Ilā, Budha begot a most righteous son.
By his own splendor he performed fully a hundred horse sacrifices; / he was renowned as Purūravas, bowed to by all the worlds.
Having worshipped the Grandfather on a pleasant peak of the Himālaya, / he then attained universal sovereignty, O king, as lord of the seven continents.
Daityas such as Keśin became his servants; / enchanted by his beauty, Urvaśī became his wife.
The earth of seven continents, along with mountains and dense forests, / was protected with righteousness by him who wished the welfare of all the world.
Fame itself bore his fly-whisk and served him in person; / by the grace of Brahmā, the lord of gods then offered him half of his throne.
Endowed with righteousness, he upheld dharma, artha, and kāma; / filled with curiosity, Dharma, Artha, and Kāma came to see him,
wishing to know his conduct: “How does he look upon us equally?” / With devotion he then offered them guest-offerings, water for the feet, and the rest.
Having brought three celestial seats adorned with gold, / he seated them and then performed worship, showing slightly more honor to Dharma.
Then both Kāma and Artha became exceedingly angry toward the king; / Artha pronounced a curse upon him: “You will meet destruction through greed!”
Kāma also said: “You will suffer madness on Gandhamādana, / resorting to the Kumāravana forest on account of separation from Urvaśī!”
Dharma, however, said: “You will be long-lived and righteous, / and your lineage, O best of kings, will endure as long as the moon and stars.
It will increase by hundreds and will not perish upon the earth; / and the madness arising from passion for Urvaśī will last sixty years.
Before long, the apsaras will once again become your obedient wife.” / Having spoken thus, they all vanished, and the king then enjoyed his kingdom.
Day after day Purūravas went to see the lord of gods. / Once, mounting his chariot, while moving in the southern sky
together with Śakra, he saw Citralekhā and Urvaśī / being carried away in the sky by Keśin, the lord of dānavas.
Having vanquished him in battle by discharging various weapons— / he by whom previously even Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, had been defeated in battle—
he attained friendship with Indra and handed Urvaśī over to him; / from then on, Pākaśāsana entered into friendship
with that very Purūravas, who surpassed all the worlds. / Gratified, the wielder of the thunderbolt said: “Let her be taken by you alone.”
For the pleasure of Purūravas, she sang of the great deed: / the drama named *Lakṣmīsvayaṃvara*, directed by Bharata.
He had commanded Menakā, Urvaśī, and Rambhā: “Dance!” / And Urvaśī danced there in rhythm in the role of Lakṣmī.
Seeing Purūravas while dancing, she was afflicted by passion / and forgot all the dramatic acting that had previously been taught.
In anger Bharata cursed her: “Because of your separation from him on the earth, / you shall become a creeper for fifty-five years!”
Then Urvaśī went to him and took him as her husband for a long time; / and at the end of enduring the curse, Urvaśī, by the son of Budha,
bore eight sons; learn their names from me: / Āyus, Dṛḍhāyus, Vaśyāyus, Balāyus, Dhṛtimat, Vasu,
Divyajāyus, and Śatāyus—all possessed of divine strength and vigor. / The son of Āyus was Nahuṣa, and likewise Vṛddhaśarman,
Raji, Daṇḍa, and Viśākha—five heroic great car-warriors. / A hundred sons were born to Raji, renowned as the Rājeyas.
Raji worshipped the stainless Nārāyaṇa; / pleased by his austerity, Viṣṇu granted a boon to the ruler of earth.
He then became victorious over gods, asuras, and humans. / Now a war between gods and asuras occurred for three hundred years,

The [battle] between Prahlāda and Śakra was terrible, and neither of them was victorious;
then the four-faced god was questioned separately by the gods and the Asuras.
“Which of these two will be victorious?” He said: “Whichever side Raji takes.” / The king was solicited for victory: “Become our ally!”
He said to the daityas: “Only if I become your master!” / That was not accepted by the asuras, but then it was accepted by the gods:
“Be our master and destroy the strength of our enemies!” / Then all those who were to be slain by the wielder of the thunderbolt were destroyed.
Gratified by his deed, Indra then assumed the position of his son; / having previously given the kingdom back to Indra, Raji departed for penance.
When Indra’s sacrificial portion and sovereignty were seized by force / by Raji’s sons, who were endowed with the qualities of ascetic power,
deprived of his kingdom and tormented by the sons of Raji, Śakra / spoke wretchedly to Vācaspati: “I am tormented by the sons of Raji.
Tormented as I am, O Bṛhaspati, I have neither sacrificial portion nor sovereignty. / O lord of intelligence, make an effort for my regaining of the kingdom!”
Thereupon Bṛhaspati made Śakra arrogant with power / through rites for pacifying the planets and through rituals of empowerment.
Then, having set out, Bṛhaspati, who knew righteousness, deluded the sons of Raji, / resorting to the doctrine of the Jinas which is outside the Veda.
The lord of intelligence caused them to fall away from the threefold Veda; / knowing that they were outside the Veda and engaged in skeptical sophistry,
Śakra struck down with his thunderbolt all of them who were excluded from righteousness. / I shall tell of the seven righteous sons of Nahuṣa:
Yati, Yayāti, Śaryāti, Uttara, Para, / Ayati, and Viyati—these seven were increasers of the lineage.
Even in youth, Yati became an ascetic yogin; / Yayāti ruled the kingdom, ever taking righteousness as his sole refuge.
Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, was his wife, / and also Devayānī of virtuous vows, the daughter of the Bhārgava.
There were five heirs of Yayāti; I shall declare them by name: / Devayānī gave birth to the son Yadu and also Turvasu;
likewise Śarmiṣṭhā gave birth to the sons Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru. / Yadu and Pūru: those two were indeed increasers of the lineage of Bharata.
I shall declare the lineage of Pūru, in which you were born, O king; / from Yadu, however, were born the Yādavas, where Bala and Keśava appeared
to lighten the burden [of the earth] and for the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas. / There were five sons of Yadu, resembling sons of the gods:
Sahasrajit, the eldest, as well as Kroṣṭu, Nīla, Añjika, and Raghu. / The heir of Sahasrajit was the king named Śatajit;
and the heirs of Śatajit were three, supremely righteous: / Haihaya, Haya, and also he who was Tālahaya.
The heir of Haihaya was renowned as Dharmanetra; / the son of Dharmanetra was Kunti, and his son was Saṃhata.
The heir of Saṃhata was the king named Mahiṣmat; / the son of Mahiṣmat was the valiant Bhadrasena.
He was the king in Vārāṇasī, as indeed told previously; / the son of Bhadrasena was the righteous Durdama.
The formidable and valorous son of Durdama was named Dhanaka; / and four sons were born to Dhanaka, renowned throughout the world:
Kṛtāgni, Kṛtavīrya, and likewise Kṛtadharma, / and Kṛtaujas was the fourth; and from Kṛtavīrya came that Arjuna.
Born with a thousand arms, the king was the lord of the seven continents; / the lord of the earth performed severe penance for ten thousand years.
Kārtavīrya worshipped Datta, born of Atri; / to him Datta, the highest among men, granted four boons.
First, that best of kings chose a thousand arms, / and fear, and restraint from contemplating unrighteousness;
having conquered the earth in battle, obtaining strength through righteousness; / and that his death should come from an extraordinary [warrior] when engaged in battle.
By him this earth, possessing seven continents and cities, / surrounded by the seven oceans, was conquered according to the rule of kṣatriyas.
And a thousand arms came into being as the wise king desired. / All the sacrifices of that mighty-armed one were endowed with abundant fees;
all their sacrificial posts were of gold, all their altars of gold, / and all were visited by gods standing adorned in celestial chariots,

and ever attended by gandharvas and apsarases. / At his sacrifice, the gandharva Nārada sang this song,

beholding the glory of the royal sage Kārttavīrya: / 'Surely no kings will ever attain the stature of Kārttavīrya
in sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valor, and sacred learning.' / Wandering over the seven continents with speed like the wind,
for eighty-five thousand years that ruler of men / was indeed the emperor of the earth with its seven continents.
He alone was the protector of cattle, he alone was the guardian of the field, / and he alone became Parjanya with rain through his yoga—that was Arjuna.
With his thousand arms, their skin hardened by the strike of bowstrings, / he shone like the autumn sun with its thousand rays.
He alone among men possessed such great splendor in Māhiṣmatī; / he would indeed confront the speed of the ocean in the rainy season.
The king played against the current for his own pleasure; / as he played, the Narmadā, garlanded with waves held back by him,
with a row of knitted brows made of waves, approached him in fear. / He alone in the lineage of Manu plunged into the great ocean;
raising its force with his hand to delight the lovely woman. / When the great ocean was churned by his thousand arms,
the great asuras dwelling in Pātāla became motionless and hid, / terrified by the churning of his thighs and dreading the production of nectar;
and the great serpents bowed down with motionless heads. / That bowman discharged arrows against Rāvaṇa;
that bowman took up his bow, and with five arrows / stupefied the arrogant lord of Laṅkā, Rāvaṇa, together with his army, by force;
having conquered him, bound him, and brought him to Māhiṣmatī, he imprisoned him. / Then I went before him, placating Arjuna;
the king released my grandson, O king, and forged a friendship with him. / The sound of the bowstrings on his thousand arms was
like the sound of the bowstring of the fire kindled at the end of the cosmic age. / Ah, the power of fate and its strength, when that Bhārgava cut down
his thousand arms in battle, as though a grove of golden palmyra trees! / For whom the powerful Vasiṣṭha, being enraged, had cursed Arjuna:
'Since my renowned forest was burned down by you, O Haihaya, / therefore another will slay you for the evil deed you committed.
Having cut off your thousand arms and crushed you with his power, a mighty / ascetic brāhmaṇa, that Bhārgava, will surely kill you.'
Thus Rāma became the slayer of that wise king by the sage's curse. / He had a hundred sons, among whom five were great chariot-warriors,
trained in weapons, powerful, heroic, righteous, and of great strength: / Śūrasena, Śūra, Dhṛṣṭa, Kṛṣṇa,
and Jayaddhvaja, who was the creator and lord of the Avanti region. / The son of Jayaddhvaja was the mighty Tālajaṅgha;
his sons were indeed a hundred, known as the Tālajaṅghas. / There were five families of those noble Haihayas:
the Vītihotras, the Bhojas, the Avantis, / the valiant Tuṇḍikeras, and the Tālajaṅghas, as they are recorded.
The son of Vītihotra was powerful, named Ananta; / his son was Durjaya, the tormentor of enemies.
Protecting his subjects righteously with good intent, the great king / was named Kārtavīryārjuna, the bearer of a thousand arms,
by whom the earth up to the ocean was conquered with his bow. / That man who recounts his name upon rising at dawn
suffers no loss of wealth and recovers what was lost. / Whoever narrates here the birth of the wise Kārtavīrya, / just as he sacrificed and just as he gave, is honored in the heavenly world.

1.13.m: Pulastya said: / Hear, O best of kings, the lineage of Kroṣṭu, comprising excellent men, / in whose family was born Viṣṇu, the uplifter of the Vṛṣṇi race.
To Kroṣṭu was born a son, Vṛjinīvat of great fame; / his son was Svāti, and Kuśaṅku was his son.
To Kuśaṅku was born a son named Citraratha; / he became renowned as Śaśabindu, a universal emperor.
In this matter, this lineage-verse was sung of him in ancient times: / Śaśabindu had a hundred times a hundred sons,
wise, handsome, and of vast wealth and brilliance. / Among those hundred principal ones, the mighty sons named after Pṛthu
were Pṛthuśravas, Pṛthuyaśas, Pṛthutejas, Pṛthūdbhava, / Pṛthukīrti, and Pṛthumati—kings belonging to Śaśabindu's line.
Those who know the Purāṇas praise Pṛthuśravas as the best. / From him was born a son, Uśanas, the tormentor of foes;
and the son of Uśanas was named Śineyu, best of men. / The son of Śineyu was known as Rukmakavaca.
Having slain [his enemies] in battle, Rukmakavaca, skilled in combat, / and archers with diverse arrows, and having obtained this earth,
the king gave sacrificial fees to the brāhmaṇas in the horse sacrifice. / From Rukmakavaca was born Parāvṛt, the slayer of enemy heroes.
His sons were born five, of great vigor and valor: / Rukmeṣu, Pṛthurukma, Jyāmagha, Parigha, and Hari.
The father settled Parigha and Hari in Videha; / Rukmeṣu became the king, and Pṛthurukma his dependent.
Banished from the kingdom by the two of them, Jyāmagha lived in a hermitage; / tranquil and residing in the hermitage, he was awakened [to action] by a brāhmaṇa.
Taking his bow, bearing a banner, and mounted on a chariot, he went to another country, / alone on the bank of the Narmadā, solely emaciated in livelihood.
Going to Mount Ṛkṣavat, he settled there, free from resentment toward others. / Jyāmagha had a wife, Śaibyā, who was advanced in years and devoted.
Although childless, the king did not think of another wife. / He won a victory in battle, and there, having captured a maiden,
he spoke to his wife in fear: 'Fair-smiling one, this is your daughter-in-law.' / When he had spoken thus, she said to him: 'Whose daughter-in-law is she?'
The king said: / 'She will be the wife of the son who will be born to you.' / By her severe austerity, that maiden bore
a fortunate son, Vidarbha, to the devoted Śaibyā advanced in years; / and on the princess, his daughter-in-law, [Vidarbha begot] the two learned sons, Kratha and Kauśika.
Afterward, Vidarbha begot a third son, Lomapāda, / supremely righteous, heroic, and skilled in battle.
Lomapāda's son was Babhru, and Babhru's son was Dhṛti; / the son of Kauśika was Cedi, and from him came the kings known as Caidyas.
The son of Vidarbha was Kratha, and his son was Kunti. / From Kunti was born Dhṛṣṭa; from Dhṛṣṭa came the majestic Sṛṣṭa.
Sṛṣṭa's son was the righteous Nivṛtti, slayer of enemy warriors. / Nivṛtti's son was Dāśārha, and his [son] was named Vidūratha.
The son of Dāśārha was Bhīma, and from Bhīma is said [to come] Jīmūta. / Jīmūta's son was Vikṛti, and his son was Bhīmaratha.
Then Bhīmaratha's son was indeed Navaratha; / and his was Daśaratha, and his son was Śakuni.
From him came Karaṃbha, and from him arose Devarāta. / The renowned king Devakṣatra came from Devarāta.
Equal to an embryo of the gods, Devakṣatra's delight was born, / named Madhu, of great splendor; from Madhu, Kuruvaśa is remembered.
From Kuruvaśa came a son, the majestic Puruhotra. / Then from Puruhotra, Aṃśu was born of Dravaṃtī, a princess of Vidarbha.
Aṃśu's wife was Vetrakī, and upon her was born / Sātvata, full of virtue, increaser of the Sātvatas' fame.
Knowing this lineage of the great-souled Jyāmagha, / one attains offspring and union with the wise King Soma.
Kausalyā bore Sātvatas, sons endowed with virtue; / their four branches [arose]—hear them in detail.
To Bhajamāna, through the Sṛñjaya princess, a son named Bhājana was born. / And from the daughter of Sṛñjaya arose the Bhājakas.
The two wives of that Bhāja bore many sons: / Nemi, Kṛkaṇa, and Vṛṣṇi, conqueror of enemy cities.
They are remembered as the Bhājakas because they were born from Bhajamāna. / Devāvṛdha, named Pṛthu, was a magnifier of friends among the Madhus.
That king was childless, and he performed supreme austerities, / yearning: 'May I have a son endowed with all good qualities!'
Fixing his mind upon Kṛṣṇa and touching the water of the Parṇāśā river, / that river approached him through his contact with the water.
As he was performing auspicious acts, the river grew sorrowful for him; / her mind filled with thought, she then came to a firm resolve:
'Becoming a woman, I shall go [to him], so that such a son / may be born of me; therefore today I shall grant him a son.'
Then, having become a maiden possessing supreme beauty, / she made herself known to the king, and then the king desired her.
Then, in the ninth month, that best of rivers bore / to Devāvṛdha a superior son, Babhru, endowed with all virtues.
Regarding this lineage, those versed in the Purāṇas recite this well-known verse, / singing the virtues of the great-souled Devāvṛdha:
'Babhru is the best of men; Devāvṛdha is equal to the gods. / Sixty, a hundred, and seventy thousand sons—
these attained immortality from Babhru and Devāvṛdha!' / Wise in sacrifices, gifts, and austerities, devoted to the sacred, firm in his vows,
handsome and of great splendor, Bhoja [ruled] over Mṛtakāvatī. / The daughter of Śarakānta bore four sons:
Kukura, Bhajamāna, Śyāma, and Kambalabarhis. / Kukura's son was Vṛṣṭi, and Vṛṣṭi's son was Dhṛti.
His was Kapotaroman, and his son was Tittiri. / He had a wise son named Bahuputra, also called Nari.
Another name of his is celebrated as Candanodakadundubhi. / His son was Abhijit, and from him was born Punarvasu.
Abhijit had previously been childless; prompted with joy by the sages, / that best of men performed a horse sacrifice for the sake of a son.
As he was walking in the middle [of the sacrificial ground], there arose from the assembly hall / Punarvasu, who was Andha, wise, knowing dharma, and a giver of sacrifices.
He had twin children, from Vasu and Arijit: / Āhuka and Āhukī, celebrated [among the people], O best of the wise!
And here they cite these verses, full of deep sentiment: / 'Of quivers, axles, armors, and chariot bodies,
and of chariots rumbling like clouds, there were ten thousand. / No Bhojas spoke untruth, nor were any not performers of sacrifices or not givers of thousands.
None was impure, none was unlearned, and none was superior to a Bhoja.' / This lineage is declared to have extended down to Āhuka.
Āhuka gave his sister Āhukī in marriage among the Avantis. / The daughter of Āhuka gave birth to two sons:
Devaka and Ugrasena, both equal to the offspring of the gods. / And sons were born to Devaka, resembling the thirty gods:
Devavān, Upadeva, Sudeva, and Devarakṣita. / Their sisters were seven, whom he gave to Vasudeva:
Devakī, Śrutadevā, Yaśodā, Śrutiśravā, / Śrīdevā, Upadevā, and the seventh was Surūpā.
Ugrasena had nine sons, of whom Kaṃsa was the eldest: / Nyagrodha, Sunāman, Kaṅka, Śaṅku, and Subhū,
and another was Rāṣṭrapāla, and Baddhamuṣṭi with Samuṣṭika. / Their sisters were five: Kasā, Kaṃsavatī,
Surabhī, Rāṣṭrapālī, and Kaṅkā—excellent women. / Ugrasena along with his offspring has been explained as sprung from Kukura.
Bhajamāna had a son, the foremost of charioteers, Vidūratha. / Rājādhideva the heroic was the son of Vidūratha.
To Rājādhideva two sons were born, honored as heroes, / devoted to the warrior's vow: Śoṇāśva and Śvetavāhana.
Śoṇāśva had five heroic sons, skilled in battle: / Śamī, Rājaśarman, Nimūrtta, Śatrujit, and Śuci.
Śamī's son was Pratikṣatra, and the son of Pratikṣatra / was Bhoja, and his son was Hṛdīka. / Hṛdīka had ten sons of dreadful valor.
Kṛtavarman was their eldest, and Śatadhanvan was the best; / Devārha, Subhānu, and the mighty Bhīṣaṇa;
Ajāta, Vijāta, Karaka, and Karaṃdhama. / To Devārha was born a wise son, Kambalabarhis.
Then he had two sons, Asamaujas and Samaujas. / To the son of Ajāta two sons were born of equal vigor.
Samaujas had three renowned and supremely righteous sons, / named respectively Sudaṃśa, Suvaṃśa, and Kṛṣṇa.
Whoever constantly recites this lineage of the Andhakas / thereby obtains a vast lineage and offspring for himself.
Gāndhārī and Mādrī were the two wives of Kroṣṭu. / Gāndhārī gave birth to Sunitra, fond of friends.
Mādrī bore a son, Yudhājit, and then Devamīḍhuṣa, / Anamitra, and Śini; these five had auspicious marks.
Anamitra's son was Nighna, and Nighna had two sons: / Prasena of great power and Śaktisena—both of them.
Prasena possessed the Syamantaka, an unsurpassed jewel, / celebrated on earth as the king of jewels.
Wearing that jewel constantly on his chest, he shone brightly. / Then Śauri asked for that supreme jewel on behalf of the king.
Govinda did not obtain it, nor did he seize it though he was capable. / Once, Prasena went out hunting adorned with it.
In a cave he heard a sound made by some creature; / then, entering that cave, Prasena came upon a bear.
The bear [assailed] Prasena, and likewise Prasena, conqueror of enemies, / assailed the bear; the two fought with each other, desiring victory.
Having slain Prasena, the bear then took the jewel. / But hearing that Prasena was killed, Govinda was suspected
by Satrājit, his brother, and likewise by the other Yādavas: / “Surely Prasena was killed by Govinda for the sake of the jewel!
Prasena went to the forest adorned with the precious jewel; / seeing him, he killed him then, since he would not yield the Syamantaka.
Keśava struck down an enemy because he would not give it up.” / Such was the rumor spread everywhere by Satrājit.
Then, after a long time, Govinda went out on a hunt again; / and by chance he came to the vicinity of the cave.
Then the mighty king of bears made a roar just as before. / Hearing that roar, Govinda entered with a sword in hand,
and saw Jāmbavant, the king of bears, endowed with great strength. / Then Hṛṣīkeśa swiftly [rushed] toward that bear with great speed;
with eyes bloodshot with rage, he seized Jāmbavant. / And seeing him as Viṣṇu, [revealed] by deeds in his Vaiṣṇava form,
the king of bears also praised him quickly with the Viṣṇusūkta. / Thereupon the Blessed One, being pleased, offered him a boon.
Jāmbavant said: / “My death at your hands by a blow of the discus is welcome and auspicious to me. / And may this maiden, my daughter, obtain you as her husband.
This jewel, which I obtained from Prasena after killing him— / let that be taken by you, O Lord; here is this jewel.”

Having been addressed thus, Keśava, having slain Jāmbavat with his discus,
his task accomplished, the mighty-armed one then gave the maiden.
Then he gave this precious jewel to Satrājit, / which had been obtained from the king of bears, in the presence of all the Yādavas.
Janārdana had been tormented by that false rumor. / Then all those Yādavas spoke to Vāsudeva:
“Indeed, it was in our minds that Prasena was killed by you.” / Satrājit had ten sons by each beautiful [wife];
one hundred renowned sons were born to him, true to their word, / and celebrated, possessing great valor; and Bhaṅgakāra was the eldest.
Satyā, Vratavatī, and Svapnā were elder sisters of Bhaṅgakāra; / they gave birth to sons, and the glorious Śinīvāla,
Abhaṅga, and Yuyudhāna; and Śini was his son. / From him [came] Yugaṃdhara; one hundred sons of his are proclaimed.
He who was named Anamitra was renowned, born of the lineage of Vṛṣṇi. / From Anamitra was born Śini, the youngest delight of the Vṛṣṇis.
And from Anamitra was born the Vṛṣṇi hero Yudhājit, / and two other heroic sons, Ṛṣabha and Citra.
Ṛṣabha obtained the faultless daughter of the king of Kāśi as his wife; / and Jayanta obtained the auspicious Jayantī as his wife.
Then a son was born to Jayanta by Jayantī, / who was ever a performer of sacrifices, very steadfast, learned, and fond of guests.
From him was born Akrūra, very clever, who gave bountiful sacrificial gifts. / Akrūra obtained the maiden gem of the Śaibya family.
He fathered eleven sons endowed with great strength: / Upalambha, Sadālambha, Utkala, Āryaśaiśava,
Sudhīra, Sadāyakṣa, Śatrughna, Vārimejaya, / Dharmadṛṣṭi, Dharma, and likewise Sṛṣṭimauli.
And they all were born as obtainers of gems. / From Akrūra were born two sons who delighted the lineage by Śūrasenā:
Devavant and Upadeva were born, regarded as gods. / On Aśvinī [were born] three [and] four sons: Pṛthu and Vipṛthu,
Aśvagrīva, Aśvabāhu, Supārśvaka, Gaveṣaṇa, / Ariṣṭanemi, Suvarcas, Sudharman, and Mṛdu,
Abhūmi, Bahubhūmi, and two daughters, Śraviṣṭhā and Śravaṇā. / A wise person who knows this false accusation against Kṛṣṇa
is never overtaken by a false accusation from anyone. / The Aikṣvākī queen gave birth to a heroic, marvelous son, Mīḍhuṣa.
From Mīḍhuṣa ten heroic men were born of Bhojā, / the first being the mighty-armed Vasudeva, named Ānakadundubhi.
Likewise Devabhāga was born, and again Devaśravas, / Anāvṛṣṭi, Kuni, Nandi, and Sakṛdyaśas,
Śyāma, and Śamīka as the seventh; and he had five excellent women: / Śrutakīrti, Pṛthā, Śrutadevī, Śrutaśravā,
and Rājādhidevī—these five were mothers of heroes. / Śrutadevī bore to the elder [Vṛddhaśarman] the Kārūṣa king.
From the Kaikeya king, King Saṃtardana was born to Śrutakīrti; / and from Śrutaśravas, Sunītha was born to the Caidya.
Born of Rājādhidevī was [Jayatsena], free from fear through righteousness. / Śūra, bound by friendship, gave Pṛthā to Kuntibhoja.
Thus Pṛthā, the sister of Vasudeva, was named Kuntī. / Kuntibhoja gave that blameless woman to Pāṇḍu as his wife.
For Pāṇḍu’s sake, that divine lady gave birth to sons of gods, great chariot-warriors: / from Dharma was born Yudhiṣṭhira; from the Wind was born Vṛkodara;
and from Indra was born Dhanañjaya, equal in prowess to Śakra, / who, born from the three persons with three portions, was a great chariot-warrior,
a doer of the gods' work and the slayer of all Dānavas; / by whom the Dānavas, invulnerable even to Śakra, were slain.
Having gained glory, he was established in heaven by Śakra. / By Mādravatī the two Aśvins were born, so we have heard:
Nakula and Sahadeva, endowed with beauty, good nature, and virtues. / The wife of Ānakadundubhi named Rohiṇī Pauravī
obtained a cherished son, Rāma, and Sāraṇa who was fond of battle, / Durdhara, Damana, Piṇḍāraka, and Mahāhanu.
Now she who was like the night of the new moon through illusion was Devakī. / On her was born the mighty-armed one who had formerly been the Lord of Creatures.
Born after him was Kṛṣṇā, Subhadrā of auspicious speech; / and Vijaya, Rocamāna, Vardhamāna, and Devala—
all these great-souled ones were born of Upadevī. / Bṛhaddevī gave birth to the great-souled Agāvaha.
On Bṛhaddevī was born himself [a son] by name Mandaka. / As the seventh son of Devakī, she bore a son named Remanta,
and Gaveṣaṇa, the fortunate one, undefeated in battles. / Formerly, while wandering in the forest for sport with Śrutadevī,
Śauri fathered an eldest son, Kauśika, on a Vaiśyā. / Śrutaṃdharā, the queen, took the fragrant one;
and the mighty son of Vasudeva [fathered] a son, Kapila. / The foremost archer became a sorrow to the people.
Saubhadra and Abhava both became endowed with great strength. / And the son of Devabhāga was Prastāva, known as wise.
To Devaśravas the foremost wise son was Bāhu, the excellent one, / from whose illustrious and noble [wife] of the Ikṣvāku line
Nivṛttaśatru, Śatrughna, and Śraddhā were born. / On Gaṇḍūṣā, Kṛṣṇa, being pleased, bestowed one hundred offspring,
and Candra, the highly fortunate, heroic, and very strong. / Rantipāla and Ranti were both the sons of Nandana.
The sons of Śamīka were four, valorous and very mighty: / Viraja, Dhanus, Vyoma, and his Sṛñjaya.
Vyoma was childless; Sṛñjaya's [son] was Dhanañjaya, / who, upon being born, attained kingship over the Bhojas and the status of a royal sage.
Whoever constantly proclaims the birth and rise of Kṛṣṇa, / or listens to it constantly, that man is freed from all sins.
Now, the god Mahādeva, formerly Kṛṣṇa, the lord of creatures— / for the sake of sport, that god was born even among men.
Through the asceticism of Vasudeva, the lotus-eyed one was born from Devakī, / four-armed, of divine form, the refuge of all beings.
Beholding the god endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark and the characteristics of the gods, / Vasudeva said to him: "Withdraw your form, O Lord.
I am afraid of king Kaṃsa; therefore I say this to you. / My six excellent sons of terrible prowess were killed by him."
Hearing Vasudeva's words, the imperishable one withdrew his form. / Having taken leave of him, the descendant of Śūra carried him to the house of the cowherd Nanda.
Having given him to the cowherd Nanda, he said: "Let him be protected. / From him, all prosperity will come to the Yādavas.
This embryo of Devakī, as soon as he slays Kaṃsa, / so long will there be supreme safety on earth, taking away its burden.
Those kings who are wicked, all of them he will slay / when the battle of the Kauravas takes place, where all the warriors assemble.
The god himself will act as the charioteer of Arjuna. / Having rid the earth of kṣatriyas, he will enjoy it when it has become a remainder.
And he will lead the entire family of Yadu to the world of the gods." / Bhīṣma said: / "Who was this Vasudeva, and who was the glorious Devakī?
And who was the cowherd Nanda, and who was Yaśodā of great vows, / who nourished Viṣṇu, and whom he addressed as 'mother'?
Who gave birth to the embryo, and who raised him?" / Pulastya said: / "The man was Kaśyapa, and Aditi is remembered as his beloved.
Kaśyapa was a portion of Brahmā, and likewise Aditi of the Earth. / Nanda is celebrated as Droṇa, and Yaśodā then was Dharā.
Then the mighty-armed one fulfilled the desires of Devakī, / which had been wished for by her previously from that unborn, great-souled one.
Not long after, that great god entered a human body; / deluding all beings, the yogin came through yoga.
When dharma and sacrifice were ruined, Viṣṇu, the all-pervading lord, [was born] in the lineage of the Vṛṣṇis / to establish the order of dharma and to destroy the asuras.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Satyā the daughter of Nagnajit, / Sumitrā, and Śaibyā, Gāndhārī, and Lakṣmaṇā,
Subhīmā, and Mādrī, Kauśalyā, and Vijayā— / and sixteen thousand others of these queens.
Rukmiṇī gave birth to sons—listen—who were skilled: / Cārudeṣṇa, heroic in battle, and the mighty Pradyumna,
Sucāru, Cārubhadra, Sadaśva, and Hrasva, / the seventh Cārugupta, Cārubhadra, and Cāruka,
the youngest Cāruhāsa, and a daughter, Cārumatī. / To Satyabhāmā were born Bhānu, Bhīmaratha, Kṣaṇa,
Rohita, and Dīptimat, Tāmrabandha, and Jalaṃdhama; / and four younger sisters were born to them.
To Jāmbavatī was born a son, Sāmba, very handsome, / the maker of the solar treatise and of the idol's temple.
The settlement at Mūlasthāna was made by that great-souled one; / by the pleased god of gods, his leprosy was destroyed.
Mitravindā gave birth to Sumitra and Cārumitra; / Mitrabāhu and Sunītha were born to Nāgnajitī.
Hear of the thousands of sons beginning with these: / eighty thousand were the sons of Vāsudeva.
The heir of Pradyumna through the princess of Vidarbha, best in intellect, / Aniruddha, a fighter in battle, was born, whose emblem is a deer.
Kāmyā, the daughter of Supārśva, obtained from Sāmba a swift [son]. / Five supreme gods of sattva nature are proclaimed.
Thirty million heroes of the noble Yādavas, / and sixty hundred thousand, full of valor and mighty,
were all born here as portions of the gods, possessing great majesty. / The asuras of great might who had been killed in the battle between gods and asuras,
born here among men, were oppressing all mortals. / For their deliverance, [these heroes] were born in the lineage of Yadu.
Of the hundred and one clans of the noble Yādavas, / Viṣṇu was the leader and was established in sovereignty.
Abiding by his command, all the Yādavas flourished." / Bhīṣma said: / "The seven sages, Kubera, and the yakṣa Maṇidhara,
Sātyaki, and Nārada, Śiva, and Dhanvantari, / and the primeval god Viṣṇu together with these deities—
for what purpose were those divine incarnations born together on earth? / How many future manifestations of this great-souled one will there be?
Why was he born in all places, here in all of them? / For what purpose was Viṣṇu born here in the lineage of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas
"Listen, O king, I will tell the secret of secrets: / how Viṣṇu of divine body is born here among men.
At the end of an age, when time has revolved and is failing, / the lord Hari, the sovereign ruler, is born among gods, asuras, and men.
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was the ruler of the three worlds; / and when the three worlds were again occupied by Bali in sequence,
there was supreme friendship between the gods and the asuras. / For ten complete periods named yugas, the world was unperturbed,
and the gods and asuras themselves stood abiding by their commands. / Bali was bound, [and then] this very fierce clash took place.
Dreadful and destructive, it was a great [conflict] between gods and asuras. / And to establish the order of dharma, he is born here among men,
due to the curse of Bhṛgu, on account of the gods and asuras." / Bhīṣma said: / "How did Hari obtain a physical body on account of the gods and asuras?
Tell me, O you of good vows, how the affair between gods and asuras happened." / Pulastya said: / "For the sake of their victory, there were very dreadful battles.
Twelve pure descents are remembered in the Manvantara. / Listen to their names in brief, as I intend to speak them.
The first is Narasiṃha, and the second is Vāmana; / the third is Varāha, and the fourth is the Churning for Nectar.
The fifth battle was the very dreadful battle over Tārakā; / the sixth is named Āḍīvaka, and the seventh was the Tripura battle;
the eighth was the Slaying of Andhaka; the ninth, the Slaying of Vṛtra; / their tenth was Dhvaja; after that, the Hālāhala;
the famous twelfth among them was the dreadful Kolāhala. / The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was destroyed by the Man-Lion;

Formerly Bali was bound by Vāmana when he strode over the three worlds;
Hiraṇyākṣa was slain in a duel over the dispute with the gods.

Standing in the ocean, he was split in two by the Boar with his tusk;
Prahlāda was defeated in battle by Indra at the churning for nectar.

And Virocana, the son of Prahlāda, was always intent on slaying Indra;
showing his valour, Indra slew him in the Tārakāmaya war.
When the gods were unable to endure the demonic Tripura, / the enemy of the Asuras deluded them in the form of a cow and drank the nectar.
The dead Asuras could not be revived again and again; / all the Dānavas were slain in the three worlds by Tryambaka.
In the slaying of Andhaka, Asuras, Piśācas, and Dānavas / were slain completely by gods, men, and ancestors.
Vṛtra, joined with the Dānavas, was slain in a terrible uproar; / he was struck down then by great Indra with Viṣṇu's assistance.
Then Vipracitti, who knew yoga, disguised by illusion, / entering for a moment, was slain along with his followers by great Indra with his thunderbolt.
All those Daityas and Dānavas together— / these twelve wars indeed took place between the gods and Asuras.
They caused the destruction of gods and Asuras, yet were truly for the welfare of the creatures. / King Hiraṇyakaśipu reigned for one hundred million years,
and moreover, seventy-two hundred-thousand, / and eighty thousand years; he was the sovereign of the three worlds.
In turn, Bali was king for one hundred million years, / and sixty thousand, and two million years.

For as long as the period of Bali's rule was proclaimed to last,
for that long a time Prahlāda lived at ease with the Asuras.
These highly glorious [kings] should be understood [to have ruled] for the victory of the Asuras. / This undisturbed threefold world was then protected by great Indra.
All this was unfulfilled for ten thousand years again, / when by rotation the threefold world was attained by the chastiser of Pāka.
Then the sacrifice abandoned the Asuras and went to the gods. / When the sacrifice had gone to the gods, the sons of Diti spoke to Kāvya.
The Daityas said: / "Our kingdom has been seized by Maghavat; the sacrifice has abandoned [us] and gone to the gods. / We are unable to remain here; let us enter Rasātala."
Spoken to thus, he consoled those dejected ones with his speech, saying: / "Do not fear, O Asuras! I shall sustain you with my own splendour.
Whatever mantras and medicinal herbs exist upon the earth, / all that resides in me, while only a quarter [is] with the gods.
And I will give all of that, which has been held by me for your sake." / Then the gods, seeing them sustained by wise Kāvya,
consulted together, agitated, desiring to seize them: / "This Kāvya indeed turns everything back from us by force.
Let us quickly go properly before he causes [us] to fall; / having forcefully conquered those who remain, let us drive them to Pātāla."
Then the gods, infuriated, advanced upon the Dānavas; / then, being struck down by them, they fled to Kāvya alone.
Then Kāvya, seeing them rapidly pursued by the gods, / gathered those who were afflicted by the gods from the gods for the sake of protection.
Seeing Kāvya standing [firm], the gods abandoned [their pursuit], free from hesitation. / Then Kāvya, having reflected upon the beneficial words of Brahmā,
then spoke to them, remembering past events: / "Your entire threefold world was seized by Vāmana with three steps.
Bali was bound, Jambha was killed, and Virocana was slain; / the great Asuras were killed by the gods in twelve battles.
By various means, the most prominent were mostly slain; / only a few remain of you, and it is my view that there should be no war.
Strategies must be devised by you; bide your time in the course of time. / I shall go to Mahādeva for mantras that bring victory.
Then, having obtained from Maheśvara mantras that are unopposed by the gods, / we will fight again with the gods, and then you will surely attain victory."
Then the Asuras, having conferred, spoke to the gods at that time: / "We have all laid down our weapons, having no armour and without chariots.
Clad in bark garments, we shall perform austerities." / The gods, hearing their speech spoken with truth then,
all turned back then, relieved of distress and delighted. / When the Daityas had laid down their weapons, the gods turned away at that time.
Then Kāvya said to them: "Remaining engaged in austerity, / devoid of arrogance and endowed with austerity, bide your time, which accomplishes the objective.
Dwelling in my father's hermitage, O Dānavas, await me." / For the sake of those Asuras, Kāvya approached Mahādeva.
Śukra said: / "O God, I desire mantras that do not exist with Bṛhaspati, / for the defeat of the gods and for the victory of the Asuras."
Spoken to thus, the God said: "Perform a vow, O Bhārgava: / for a full thousand years, [inhaling] smoke of grains, with your head turned downwards.
If you drink [smoke], may there be welfare to you; then you will obtain the mantras." / Having consented, saying "So be it," Śukra, the delight of Bhṛgu,
touching both feet of the God, spoke the word: "Certainly. / I shall perform the vow, O God, as instructed by you today, O Lord."
Instructed by the God of gods, the Bhārgava sage performed [it]. / Then, when that Śukra had departed for the welfare of the Asuras,
Kāvya performed celibacy under Maheśvara for the sake of mantras. / Having learned of that breach of former policy, the kings [lived] at ease then.
Taking advantage of this vulnerability, the gods then in anger rushed upon them, / all clad in armour and bearing weapons, led by Bṛhaspati.
Seeing the gods again with weapons seized, the hordes of Asuras / suddenly all sprang up terrified and spoke these words to them.
The Daityas said: / "We have laid down our weapons, O gods, while our teacher has undertaken a vow. / Having given us assurance of safety, you have come desiring to slay us!
We are all without anger, staying with our weapons abandoned, / wearing rags and black antelope skins, inactive and without possessions.
We are not able to conquer the gods in battle in any way. / Without fighting, we shall seek refuge with Kāvya's mother.
Let us make known this distress until our guru returns; / and when Śukra has returned, clad in armour and with weapons we shall fight."
Having spoken thus to one another, terrified, they sought refuge / with Kāvya's mother, and she granted them freedom from fear.
"Do not fear! Do not fear! Cast away fear, O Dānavas! / As long as you dwell in my presence, no fear should befall you."
Seeing them protected by her, the gods then / forcefully assailed those Asuras without considering strength and weakness.
Then, seeing those Asuras being struck down by the gods at that time, / the goddess, enraged, said to the gods: "I shall bewilder you with sleep!"
Having collected all the materials, she then released sleep; / endowed with yoga and rich in austerity, the goddess forcefully immobilised them.
Then, seeing Indra immobilised, the gods, as if stupefied, / fled from there, terrified upon seeing Indra subdued.
When the hosts of gods had gone, Viṣṇu spoke to Indra. / Viṣṇu said: / "Enter into me, may there be welfare to you; I shall protect you, O best of the gods!"
Addressed thus, Puraṃdara then entered Viṣṇu. / Seeing him protected by Viṣṇu, the goddess, enraged, spoke these words:
"Here, O Maghavat, I shall burn you along with Viṣṇu by force! / Let all creatures look on; let the power of my austerity be seen!"

Overcome by her, those two gods, Indra and Viṣṇu, were troubled.
Viṣṇu spoke to Indra, [asking] how he might be released along with him.

Indra said, "Slay her indeed, O lord, before she burns us both!
I am especially overpowered; slay her, slay [her] without delay!"

Then Viṣṇu, having looked at her, found himself in distress regarding the killing of a woman;
then the lord, reflecting upon Śakra who was in distress, swiftly [acted].

Then, seized by haste, acting quickly, filled with fear,
Viṣṇu understood the cruel intent of that goddess.

Enraged, taking up his discus, out of fear he severed her head.
Seeing that terrible killing of a woman, the lord Bhṛgu was enraged.

Viṣṇu was then cursed by Bhṛgu when his wife was slain.
Bhṛgu said:
"Since you, knowing dharma, have slain a woman who ought not to be killed,

therefore you will surely be born seven times among men."
Then, because of that curse, whenever dharma is lost again and again,

he is born here among men for the welfare of the world.
Then, having spoken to Viṣṇu, he himself took up that head;

having brought the body and holding it with his hand, he spoke these words.
Bhṛgu said:
"You, O goddess, were slain by Viṣṇu; I revive you.

If all dharma is known or practiced by me,
by that truth live, if I speak the truth!"

Then, sprinkling her with cold water, he said, "Live, live!"
When he had spoken thus, the goddess was then brought back to life.

Then all beings, seeing her as if risen from sleep,
upon seeing her, cried out on every side, "Well done! Well done!"

Thus brought back by that Bhṛgu then,
the goddess [revived] while the gods looked on; it was indeed like a marvel.

His wife was revived again by the unperturbed Bhṛgu.
And seeing this, Indra found no peace, out of fear of Kāvya again.

Then, keeping watch, Indra spoke these words to Jayantī;
desiring conciliation, the chastiser of Pāka spoke to his own daughter:

Indra said:
"Indeed, this Kāvya is performing a terrible vow to bring about the downfall of Indra.
By that, my daughter, I have been made exceedingly agitated in mind by that intelligent one.

With various agreeable attentions, unwearied,
worship that twice-born one, my daughter, in such a way that he may be pleased.

Go, you are given to him; make an effort for my sake!"
Thus addressed, Jayantī accepted the word of her father.

She went to where he was standing, having undertaken that terrible austerity.
Seeing him hanging upside-down, drinking the smoke of chaff,

being purified [and tormented] by the yakṣa Kuṇḍadhāra,
the goddess, seeing that Kāvya striving and steadfast,

toiling for the destruction of his enemies, reduced to a feeble state,
she then carried out toward Kāvya the words spoken by her father.

Praising him with agreeable words, speaking sweetly,
serving him at the proper time with massages that brought pleasure to his skin,

serving him in manners agreeable to the practice of his vow for many years,
when this terrible vow of smoke had been completed after a thousand years,

Śiva was pleased and gratified him with a boon.
Maheśvara said:
"This vow has been performed by you alone, by no one else.

Therefore, by austerity, intellect, sacred learning, and strength,
and by splendor, you alone will surpass all the gods.

Whatever [knowledge] exists in me, O brahmin, delight of Bhṛgu,
I will give all that to you; it must not be told by you to anyone.

What need of much speaking? You shall be invulnerable!"
Having granted those boons to that descendant of Bhṛgu again and again,

he granted him lordship over creatures, lordship over wealth, and invulnerability.
Having obtained these boons, Kāvya's hair bristled with joy.

Having thus addressed the lord of gods, the blue-and-red lord,
the wise one then bowed to him with folded hands.

Then, when the god had vanished, he spoke thus to Jayantī:
"Whose [daughter] are you, fortunate woman, or who are you, grieving when I am afflicted?

Possessed of great austerity, why do you seek to win me over?
Steadfast with this devotion, modesty, and self-restraint,

and with affection, fair-hipped one, I am pleased, O woman of fair complexion!
What do you desire, fair-hipped one? What wish of yours has arisen?

I will fulfill it for you today, even if it should be very difficult to accomplish."
Thus addressed, she said to him: "You ought to know through your austerity;

for what I desire to do, O holy one, you yourself tell truthfully."
Thus addressed, looking with his divine eye, he said to her:

O fair-hipped woman, passionate lady, you desire union with me
for a hundred years, invisible to all living beings."

O goddess, dark as a blue lotus, worthy of the best, lovely-eyed one,
you choose these desires; I grant them indeed, sweet-spoken one.

"So be it; let us go to my house, O intoxicated, radiant woman!"
Then Uśanas, having arrived home together with Jayantī,

that Bhārgava of strict vows lived together with that goddess for a hundred years,
invisible to all creatures through his illusory power.

Knowing that Śukra had returned, having attained his purpose, all the sons of Diti,
eager to see him, joyfully approached his home.

When they went, they did not see their teacher concealed by illusory power,
and not knowing his mark, [they said,] "Our teacher does not come today."

Thus they all returned to their own dwellings as they had come.
Then all the hosts of gods, having gone, spoke to the descendant of Aṅgiras:

"O venerable one, go to the abode of the Dānavas and, having bewildered that army there,
bring it under your own control very quickly; act in that way!"

Dhiṣaṇa said to those gods, "I will go in just this way";
having gone by that means, Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas, was brought under control.

Assuming the form of Śukra, he stayed there and performed the office of family priest.
When he had stayed for a full hundred years, Uśanas arrived.

Then Bṛhaspati was seen in the assembly hall by the sons of Danu:
"Only one Uśanas was here; why has a second one arrived here?

There is a very great wonder here, and a quarrel will surely take place.
What will this person say, who has positioned himself at the door?

And what will our teacher say, who sits here in the assembly?"
While those sons of Danu were thus chattering, Kavi arrived.

Seeing Bṛhaspati seated there, wearing his own form,
he spoke these words in anger: "Why have you come here?

You are bewildering my disciples; is this fitting for you, O teacher of the gods?
Confused, they do not recognize you, surely bewildered by your illusory power.

Therefore, O brahmin, this violation of another's disciples is not fitting for you.
Go to your own world of the gods; remain [there], and you will obtain dharma.

My disciple Kaca was slain formerly by the foremost of the Dānavas;
he was your son seeking sacred learning, O brahmin; but your coming here is improper!"

Hearing his words, the teacher smiled and said:
"There are thieves on earth who steal the property of others;

such as these, thieves of form and body, have not been seen!
Formerly, because of the slaying of Vṛtra, Indra incurred the sin of killing a brahmin;

it was set aside by you by means of the Lokāyatika doctrine.
I know you as the son of Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, teacher of the gods,

who have arrived wearing my form! Behold, all Dānavas:
this one has arrived to bewilder you through the machinations of Viṣṇu!"
"Therefore, bind him with chains and cast him into the salt sea!" / Then Śukra spoke once again to the chaplain of the gods:
"Deluded indeed by him, you Dānavas will go to destruction! / O lord of the Dānavas, I have been deceived here by that wicked soul!
Why have you abandoned me and made another your family priest? / This is none other than Bṛhaspati, teacher of the gods and son of Aṅgiras!
You have been deceived, there is no doubt, for the benefit of the gods. / Abandon him, noble one, who brings victory to the side of your enemies!
Earlier, O lord, having instructed [you], I departed out of fear; / standing in the midst of water, I was swallowed by Mahādeva Śambhu.
I remained in his belly for a full hundred years; / and from his belly, in the form of semen (śukra), I was discharged through his penis.
The god, granter of boons, said to me: 'Śukra, choose your desired boon!' / O king, I chose a boon from the god of gods who bears the Pināka bow:
'Whatever desires are thought of in my heart, whatever boons dwell in my mind, / let all of them be mine through your grace, O Śaṅkara!'
Saying 'So be it,' I was sent by the god to your presence. / In the meantime, this Bṛhaspati became your family priest.

"You have been seen, O lord of the Dānavas; listen to the truth that was spoken by me."
Then Bṛhaspati spoke these words to Prahlāda.
"I do not know him, whether god, Dānava, or man, / who has assumed my form, O king, and come to deceive you!"
Then all those Dānavas, crying "Well done! Well done!", said: / "He is our former family priest, let him be whoever he is.
We have no need of this one; let him go back the way he came!" / Angered, Kāvya cursed the assembled lords of the Dānavas:
"Since I have been cast off by you, likewise, before long, / may I see you all stripped of glory, devoid of life, living lives of misery,
and overtaken by terrible misfortune, very soon, in every way!" / Having spoken thus, Kāvya departed at will to the ascetic grove.
When that Śukra had departed, Bṛhaspati remained there; / protecting the Dānavas there, he stayed for some time.
Then, after a great length of time had passed, O king, / all the Dānavas assembled together and questioned their teacher:
"In this worthless world of saṃsāra, grant us some knowledge / by which we may attain liberation through your grace, O observer of good vows!"
Then the teacher of the gods, who was disguised in the form of Kāvya, said: / "I too had this same thought earlier, which you have now expressed.
Be at leisure together, purified and concentrated in mind! / I shall tell you, Daityas, the knowledge that surely grants liberation.
This Vedic revelation, known by the names Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, / exists by the grace of Agni; but it causes suffering to living beings here.
Sacrifices and ancestral rites are performed by petty men intent upon their own worldly ends. / The Vaiṣṇava dharmas, as well as those instituted by Rudra,
are evil practices performed together with wives, filled mostly with violence, though thought beneficial. / How will Rudra, who is half-woman, attain liberation,
surrounded by hosts of ghosts and adorned with many bones? / There is neither heaven nor liberation here; beings only suffer in this manner.
How will Viṣṇu, who is committed to violence, attain liberation? / And Brahmā, composed of the quality of passion (rajas), feeds upon his own creation.
Moreover, divine sages and whoever else adhere to the Vedic side / are largely violent, always cruel, meat-eaters, doing evil.
The gods drink liquor, while these Brahmins eat meat; / by such dharma, who will go to heaven, and how will anyone attain liberation?
And whatever action such as sacrifice, or traditional rites like the ancestral offerings— / there is no emancipation whatsoever where this revelation is heard.
If by performing a sacrifice, killing a beast, and making a mire of blood, / one goes to heaven, then by what does one go to hell?
If satisfaction is produced in one person when food is eaten here by another, / then one should give an ancestral offering for a traveler, and he need not take food along.
Brahmins who [once] traveled in the sky have fallen from eating meat; / for them there is no heaven, nor any liberation here, O Dānavas!
Life is dear to every creature that is born; / how could a wise man eat flesh that is like his own flesh?

How can these creatures born of a womb resort to the womb? / How will they go to heaven by copulation, O lord of the Dānavas? / Where purification is done with clay and ash, what kind of purification can that be?
See how perverse this world is, O Dānava! / When urine and feces are discharged, purification is done on the penis and anus,
but there is no application [of purification] on the mouth with clay or water! / Or when food is eaten, O king, why is no purification performed
on the anus and penis in the same way? This custom is completely contradictory. / Where washing is prescribed, they do not do it at all!
In ancient times, Soma abducted Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati; / Budha was born as a son from her, yet the teacher took her back again!
Indra himself seized Ahalyā, the wife of the sage Gautama; / see what kind of dharma this is!
This and other sinful practices are seen in the world. / Where dharma is of such a kind, what can be considered the highest truth?
Speak, O lord of the Dānavas, speak further, and I shall tell you!" / Hearing the teacher's words, which seemed full of highest truth,
their curiosity was aroused, feeling detached from the ocean of worldly existence. / The Dānavas said: / "Initiate us all, O teacher, who have taken refuge in devotion!
So that we may not fall into delusion again by your command. / We have become utterly detached from worldly existence, which bestows only grief and delusion.
Deliver us all, O teacher, from the well by pulling our hair! / To what deity should we go for refuge, O best of Brahmins?
Reveal to those who have surrendered the true deity, O wise one! / Through remembrance, fasting, meditation, and concentration,
and when worship and offerings are made, emancipation is indeed attained. / We have become detached from family; we will not strive here anymore!"
Thus addressed by those foremost sons of Danu, the disguised teacher / pondered that task: "How shall I do this?
How can these sinful beings be made dwellers of hell, / cast outside the Veda by derision, and made laughingstocks in the three worlds?"

Having spoken thus, O king, Dhiṣaṇa meditated upon Keśava;
knowing his thought, Janārdana [created] Māyāmoha.
and spoke these words to Bṛhaspati: / 'This Māyāmoha will delude all those Daityas
"Out of grace for you and pleased by your devotion, this yogin has come here— / naked (sky-clad), shaven-headed, carrying peacock feathers.

When this was said by the guru, Māyāmoha afterward spoke these words:
"O lords of the Daityas, established in asceticism, speak!"
Do you desire the fruit of your ascetic tapas for this world, or for the other world?" / The Dānavas said: / "Ascetic practice is indeed accepted by us for obtaining the merit of the other world."

This was undertaken by us; what else is meant to be said there?
The naked ascetic said:
‘Carry out my words, if you desire liberation.

All this is of the Arhat, an unobstructed gate to liberation.
This [path] is worthy of liberation through dharma; none other is higher than this.

Remaining right here, you will go to heaven and also to liberation.’
In this way, by many such [assertions] devoid of the true view of liberation,

those Daityas were expelled from the Vedic path by Māyāmoha:
‘This is for dharma; this is for adharma; this is real, and this is unreal;

this is indeed for liberation; this does not grant liberation;
this is exceedingly the supreme reality, and this is not the supreme reality;

this is a duty; this is indeed not a duty; no, it is clear that this is it;
this is the dharma of the sky-clad, and this is the dharma of those with many garments.’

Since those various specious arguments were proclaimed to them by Māyāmoha,
therefore all the Daityas were made to abandon their own duties, O king.

Since they were told by Māyāmoha, ‘Be worthy of my dharma,’
they resorted to that dharma, and on that account became followers of the Arhat (Ārhatas).

Having completely abandoned the path of the three Vedas, those asuras were made to conform to it
by Māyāmoha; and in that manner others were instructed by them.

By them still others, and others by those, and in like manner others by one another,
all standing firm in their assembly, declaring: ‘Salutations to the Arhat!’

In a few days, the three Vedas were largely abandoned by those Daityas.
And again, wearing red garments, Māyāmoha, having subdued his gaze,

went to other asuras and spoke to them in sweet words:
‘If you desire heaven, or even if [you desire] nirvāṇa,

then enough with these wicked dharmas such as the slaughter of animals! Understand:
know that all this without remainder consists of consciousness alone.

Understand my words properly, as it has been spoken here by the wise:
This world is without foundation, completely devoted to erroneous knowledge,

exceedingly tainted by passion and other [vices], and wanders in the distress of cyclic existence.’
He delivered various kinds of discourse directed toward their liberation.

In whatever way he spoke against the dharma, so they abandoned it:
some speaking abuse of the Vedas, others of the gods, O king,

others of the collection of sacrificial rituals, and likewise others of the twice-born:
‘This statement that violence leads to dharma does not stand to reason!

Can oblations burnt in fire yield fruits, O wise ones?
If the attainment of heaven is desired for an animal slain in sacrifice,

why then is the sacrificer’s own father not slain there?
If a man’s satisfaction arises from what is eaten by another,

then one might offer a śrāddha to a traveler, and travelers would carry no provisions.
Having attained godhood through many sacrifices, Indra enjoys himself;

if [the fire-wood] is wood such as Śamī, then a grass-eating beast is better!’
Realizing that this word was unworthy of faith by the people,

ignoring [the Vedas], let the speech uttered by me be pleasing for your welfare:
‘For authoritative statements do not fall down from the sky, O great asuras!

Words endowed with reason should be accepted by me and by others like you.’
The Dānavas said:
‘In the doctrine of truth, we have all taken refuge in you with devotion.

Bestow your favor today, if you are pleased [with us], O Lord;
we shall gather materials in every way, suitable for initiation,

by which, through your grace, liberation may quickly be in our hands.’
Then Māyāmoha said to all those asuras at that time:

‘He who has surrendered to my teaching—my guru of foremost intellect,
the best of beings, will give initiation to you at my command.

Initiate these [disciples], O brāhmaṇa, my children, at my word!’
When Moha had gone, those Dānavas spoke these words to the Bhārgava:

‘Give [us] initiation, O noble one, which releases from all cyclic existence.’
Saying ‘So be it,’ Uśanas said to the Daityas: ‘Let us go to the Narmadā.

Ho, abandon your clothes! I shall administer your initiation.’
Thus, O Bhīṣma, those Dānavas were made sky-clad asuras there
by the wise Āṅgirasa in the form of a Bhṛgu.
Giving them an emblem of peacock feathers and a lovely garland of guñjā beads,

he then performed the pulling out of the hair on their heads.
And the pulling out of hair is the supreme means of achieving dharma:

the god Dhanada, lord of wealth, from the pulling out of hair
and from constantly wearing this attire, attained supreme perfection.

‘Permanence is obtained in this very way,’ as the Arhat himself declared in the past.
‘Through the pulling out of hair, godhood is indeed attained by mortals here;

why should one not do it, therefore, since it grants great merit?
Indeed, it is the desire of the gods: “When, in the mortal world,

in this land of Bhārata, might our birth be in a family of lay disciples (śrāvakas)?
We would bind ourselves to austerity preceded by the pulling out of hair!”’

And the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras, who were placed in front by them,
shaded by the king of serpents, showing the path of meditation—

praising him with recitation of mantras, heaven will be in the hands of the Arhats,
or liberation will surely come; what doubt is spoken of here?

‘When might we become ṛṣis, equal in splendor to the sun and fire,
free from passion, having recited the fivefold mantra in that way?

Likewise, for those of meritorious deeds who practice austerity and have reached death through the course of time,
the head is broken with a stone.

When indeed will our dwelling be in a desolate wilderness?
And the śrāvakas, focused in mind, will whisper into our ears:

“O ṛṣi, you must not depart, because you follow the path of liberation!
Whatever positions have been obtained, and those that yield a livelihood,

must be abandoned by you, and our word is indeed true!”
By our austerity and various observances,

go to the supreme abode and that path of liberation which the wise,
ascetics endowed with austerity, find through a devotional disposition.

Where there is restraint of the senses and compassion toward living beings at all times,
that is called the dharma of austerity; everything else is mere mockery.

Knowing this, you must attain and reach the supreme state
to which the Tīrthaṅkaras went, the destination to which the yogins have gone.’

Thus indeed formerly the deities, Vidyādharas, and great serpents
contemplated day and night those wishes and desires.

‘If your desire is directed toward detachment from cyclic existence,
then abandon your wives, who are bolts across the path to heaven.

How can you resort to the womb in which your father went?
How can living beings eat meat, which is like their own flesh?’

Then those terrifying Dānavas all spoke these words to their guru:
‘Initiate us, O noble one, who stand before you as your children!’

Having done so, the family priest said to them with the traditional vow:
‘Obeisance is never to be made by you to other gods.

Food is to be eaten at one place in the hollow of the hands;
water resting in that place must be free from hair and insects.

Pleasant and unpleasant must be treated as equal; [food] must never be impaired by the sight of another;
it must be eaten according to this conduct, O lord; act thus!

United together, you will thus share in liberation.’
Having spoken thus and imposed vows on those best of Danu’s sons,

Dhiṣaṇa, O king, went to the heavenly world of the gods;
he reported all that had been done and caused to be done to the Dānavas.

Then those Asuras went and dwelt along both banks of the Narmadā;
having seen those Dānavas there deprived of Prahlāda,
Then the king of the gods, delighted, spoke indeed to Namuci, / to Hiraṇyākṣa, who destroyed sacrifices, destroyed dharma, and reviled the Vedas,
to the rākṣasa of cruel deeds, to Praghasa, and to Vighasa, / to Muci, and likewise to Bāṇa, or even to Virocana,
to Mahiṣākṣa, Bāṣkala, Pracaṇḍa, and Caṇḍaka, / to Rocamāna, the terrifying Suṣeṇa, best of the Dānavas.
Seeing these and other chiefs of the Dānavas, he then spoke: / Indra said: / 'O lords of Dānavas, born in former times, you once ruled in heaven.
How now has this vow destructive of the Vedas / been undertaken by you, naked, with shaven heads and carrying water pots,
bearing peacock-feather banners? Why indeed do you remain here?' / The Dānavas said: / 'We have abandoned all the nature of asuras and stand in the dharma of the ṛṣis.
We perform acts causing an increase in dharma toward all creatures. / Enjoy the entire kingdom of the three worlds, Śakra, and go [your way].'
Saying 'So be it,' Maghavan went back to heaven. / Thus were they all deluded by the priest of the gods, O Bhīṣma.
The best of the Dānavas remained after reaching the Narmadā river. / When he learned [of it], they were all enlightened by Śukra about the incident.

Then they again set their cruel mind on seizing the three worlds.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, named 'The Deeds of the Avatāras,' in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

1.14.m: Bhīṣma said: / 'How was Arjuna, the slayer of enemy heroes, born from three persons? / And how is Karṇa celebrated as maiden-born and as the son of a charioteer?
How did their boon arise from their very nature? Tell me that. / My curiosity is great; you ought to tell it to me.'
Pulastya said: / 'Formerly, when his head was severed, Brahmā, overcome by great anger, / wiped the sweat produced on his forehead and struck it on the ground.
From the sweat was born an ear-ringed warrior, with bow and great quiver, / equipped with a thousand armors, who said: "What shall I do?"
Viriñci said to him, pointing forcefully to Rudra: / "Let this evil-minded one be slain, so that he is not born again!"
Hearing Brahmā's words and raising his bow behind him, / he set out after the great lord, arrow in hand, with a terrifying gaze.
Seeing that exceedingly fierce man, the three-eyed god, frightened of him, / fled in haste and went to Viṣṇu's hermitage.
"Save me, save me, O Viṣṇu, slayer of enemies, from this man! / A wicked, terrifying [being] in the form of a mleccha has been created by Brahmā.
Act so that the angry one does not kill me, O lord of the world!" / Having bewildered that man with a roaring sound of "huṃ",
the lord invisible to all creatures, whose self is yoga, the all-seeing one, / Keśava comforted Virūpākṣa who had arrived there.
Then, having bowed down upon the ground, he was seen by the god Viṣṇu. / Viṣṇu said: / "You are my grandson, O Rudra. What desire of yours shall I fulfill?"
Seeing the god Nārāyaṇa, he said, "Give alms!" / showing in front of him a skull, blazing with fierce splendor.
Looking at Rudra with a skull in his hand, Viṣṇu thought: / "Who else could be a worthy beggar now for the giving of alms?"
Resolving, "This one is worthy," he offered his right arm. / The moon-crested god pierced it with a very sharp trident.
Then a stream of blood flowed from the arm of the lord, / resembling liquid gold, as if fashioned of a flame of fire.
Begged for by Śambhu, it fell into the skull, / straight, rapid, violent, touching the sky in its rush.
Fifty yojanas in length, ten yojanas in breadth, / it flowed from Hari's arm for a thousand divine years.
For that long time that lord took the alms as a beggar, / given by Nārāyaṇa in that excellent vessel, the skull.
Then Nārāyaṇa spoke these supreme words to Śambhu: / "Is the vessel full or not?" Then indeed the supreme lord,
Hara, whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire, adorned by the crescent moon, / having heard Hari's words roaring like a rain-cloud,
directing his gaze into the skull with his three eyes at Janārdana, / stirring it with his finger, said: "The skull is filled."
Hearing that speech of Śiva, Viṣṇu withdrew the stream. / Then the lord with his own finger stirred the blood of Hari
for a thousand divine years with the cast of his glances. / Then, as the blood was churned, a dense mass, a bubble gradually formed,
and then arose a crowned figure with a bow, / a pair of quivers bound, with the shoulders of a bull, wearing finger-guards,
a man resembling fire, visible in the skull. / Seeing him, the venerable Viṣṇu spoke these words to Rudra:
"O Bhava, who is this man who has appeared in the skull, O Bhava?" / Hearing Hari's words, the lord said to him: "O Lord, listen!
This man is named Nara, the best among knowers of supreme weapons. / Because he was addressed by you as 'Nara', he shall therefore be Nara.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, both will be renowned in the age, / in battle, in the duties of the gods, and in the protection of the worlds.
He will be born from all that is Nārāyaṇa, and therefore he will be Nara. / Furthermore, of great splendor, he will assist you in the slaying of asuras.
A sage in the examination of knowledge, he will be a conqueror in the world. / This divine, exceedingly brilliant fifth head of Brahmā,
derived from the glowing splendor of Brahmā, from the blood of your arm, / and from the fall of my gaze—the three splendors which exist,
born from their union, he will conquer the enemy in battle. / Those who will be invulnerable and others difficult to vanquish,
and those who are terrible to Śakra and the immortals, he will terrify them." / Having spoken thus, Śambhu stood, and Hari was amazed at that time.
Standing right there in the skull, placing his hands together in reverence at his head, / that noble-minded hero praised Hara and Keśava.
He said to the two, "What shall I do?" and having spoken, stood bowed down. / The glorious Hara said to him: "A man has been created by Brahmā
with his own splendor, bow in hand; you must slay him!" / Having spoken thus to the man who held his hands joined in reverence and praised him, Śaṅkara,
taking his two hands joined in that very manner, / lifting him out of the skull, spoke words again:
"This is that fierce man who was made known to you by me, / who has been plunged into a stupor-sleep wrought by Viṣṇu's roaring.
Awaken him quickly!" Having spoken thus, Hara vanished / before the eyes of Nārāyaṇa. Then, by this Nara,
struck by his left foot, that mighty one stood up. / Then a great battle took place between the sweat-born and the blood-born.
The whole surface of the earth was made to resound with the twang of bows strung. / One armor of the sweat-born was stripped off by the blood-born.
Thus, as the two joined in battle, two divine years / passed away as they fought, the sweat-born and the blood-born, O king.
Seeing the two-armed blood-born and the sweat-born in conflict, / Vāsudeva pondered and went to the supreme abode of Brahmā.

With agitation Madhusūdana spoke thus to Brahmā:
“O Brahmā, today this sweat-born one was struck down by the blood-born one.”

Hearing this, distressed Brahmā said to Madhusūdana:
“O Hari, in this present birth let this man of mine live, grant him life!”

Pleased by this, Viṣṇu spoke to him: “So it shall be.”
Having gone to the battlefield of the two, he stopped them and said to both of them:

“In another birth, at the junction between the Kali and Dvāpara [ages],
when a great battle arises between you, there I will unite you two.”

Then summoning the lord of planets and the lord of gods, Viṣṇu
said: “These two auspicious men are to be protected by my command.

O thousand-rayed one, this sweat-born one is your own portion on the surface of the earth;
he must be brought down at the end of the Dvāpara for the success of the gods' purpose.

In the lineage of the Yadus there will be a very powerful [king] named Śūra;
his daughter named Pṛthā will be matchless in beauty on earth.

That fortunate woman will be born for the accomplishment of the purpose of the gods;
Durvāsas will give her a boon consisting of a collection of mantras:

‘Whichever god you invoke with devotion through this mantra,
O lady, by his grace a son will be born to you.’

Seeing you at sunrise, desiring you, having menstruated,
and standing seized by anxious thought, she should be approached by you, O sun.

In her womb, this one will be born as an unmarried maiden's son, delighting Kuntī;
